newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S SERIAL KILLER PROCLAIMS INNOCENCE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S SERIAL KILLER PROCLAIMS INNOCENCE.

text.p: One of South Africa's most wanted men in recent history, alleged serial killer and rapist Moses Sithole, pleaded not guilty on Monday to 38 murders and 40 rapes.

Sithole, 32, is alleged to have lured and killed his victims, mostly black women, from areas in and around the commercial heartland of Johannesburg between 1987 and 1995, under the guise of giving them jobs.

In a grey suit, Sithole listened intently through an interpreter as prosecutors told the packed Pretoria Supreme Court they would present a DNA analysis of his semen and that found on some of the rape victims as evidence.
Prosecutor Retha Meintjies described the DNA evidence as "almost 100 percent reliable" and would prove Sithole had engaged in multiple murder and rape.
Sithole, limping and grimacing with pain from a leg injury, did not look at the gallery, jam-packed with parents and sympathisers of his alleged victims.
Court documents said many of the dead women had been tied up with their own underwear and had died of "ligature strangulation".
Sithole's alleged modus operandi involved making an appointment to accompany the women to their promised place of work, usually in an area unknown to them.
He would then take them along a bushy route saying it was a short-cut. This is where he would then rape and strangle them, the prosecution says.
One of the murder victims was a two-year-old son of a woman who was raped and killed.
Sithole is alleged to be the worst murderer uncovered to date in South Africa, an extremely violent society that has spawned a row of serial killers in the last few years.
Before the 20-minute hearing a group of protesters had stood outside the court, singing in the local Sotho language: "Sithole, why are you killing us?".
A spokeswoman for the protesters said they would visit Sithole's wife at home and pray for her. "We are women...she is a woman," Masechaba Mabaso told Reuters.
"She is scared to come here because she thinks people will kill her. We are going to her house to pray for her." About
350 witnesses are expected to testify in a landmark trial set to last many months.
